balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For China Feihe Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For China Feihe Limited: this is understated -- Feihe holds most of its liquidity in structured deposits and long-term bank deposits sitting outside this line. See the chart below for the full picture the DCF actually uses.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

cashLikeStack.title: Cash-like assets and debt
cashLikeStack.content:
Feihe parks most of its balance sheet in three buckets: cash & equivalents, structured deposits (current, FVTPL wealth-management products) and long-term bank deposits. Together these dwarf total debt, which is small and mostly short-term bank borrowings plus lease liabilities.

For China Feihe Limited: the DCF's net-cash figure (cash + structured deposits + long-term deposits, less total debt) is roughly RMB15.8bn at the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date -- about 85% of the market price per share. Structured deposits turned over roughly RMB7-8bn in redemptions and purchases in FY2025, so the DCF treats them as cash-like rather than illiquid investments, but their underlyings (money-market, interbank, bonds and some trust/insurance-linked instruments per the FY2025 annual report) are not risk-free.

What to watch:

  • Falling PRC interest rates compressing the "other income" this pile generates (already visible in FY2025 and H1 FY2026)
  • Whether structured deposits keep rolling over on schedule rather than being locked up
  • Capital-return decisions (buybacks, dividends of at least 30% of net profit) drawing this pile down over time

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For China Feihe Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For China Feihe Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For China Feihe Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For China Feihe Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For China Feihe Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For China Feihe Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

revenueMix.title: Revenue by product line
revenueMix.content:
Feihe reports three product lines: infant formula (super-premium, premium and regular milk powder), other dairy (adult milk powder, liquid milk) and nutritional supplements (mainly the U.S. Vitamin World retail business).

For China Feihe Limited: infant formula is still ~88% of revenue and is the structurally declining line -- FY2025 infant formula revenue fell 16.8% YoY as management cited "intensified industry competition," while China's 0-3 age cohort has shrunk roughly 37% since 2020. Other dairy is growing fastest (RMB607m to RMB2,061m, FY2020-FY2025) but carries only ~1% gross margin in FY2025, so it cannot yet offset the infant-formula decline in profit terms even as it does in revenue.

What to watch:

  • Whether infant formula stabilises or keeps declining (H1 FY2026 turned positive, +2.3% YoY group revenue)
  • Other dairy and nutritional supplements growing in dollars but staying thin-margin
  • Only disclosed at full-year reporting, so no interim granularity

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For China Feihe Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
